NEW YORK (CNN) -- Olympic gold medalist Michael Phelps has acknowledged he engaged in "regrettable" behavior and "demonstrated bad judgment," after a British newspaper published a photograph of the swimmer smoking from a bong. Sports attorney Ryan Smith thinks Michael Phelps should speak to public about his opposition to drug use. Ryan Smith, a sports attorney and BET talk show host, on Monday spoke to John Roberts on CNN's "American Morning" about how the incident could affect Phelps' career. John Roberts: What was your reaction to news of this picture of Michael Phelps surfacing? Ryan Smith: The thing with Michael Phelps is, he's not only been an outspoken athlete against drugs so he's done a lot of testing, he's been supportive of WADA, which is the World Anti-Doping Agency. But he's really a guy of high character. So you look at this, and my first thought was, "What about his endorsement deals? What's going to happen in those?" A lot of endorsement deals have clauses that say that you can't do bad actions like this, not only crimes, but just things that you do bad in public could result in the termination of your contract. So he could lose a lot of money on this. Roberts: Now he never really admitted to smoking marijuana. ... The United States Olympic Committee isn't going to sanction him, it looks like, but did call his actions disappointing. But to the greater issue that you were talking about, in terms of his endorsement deals, do you think anybody is going to say, well, this is the straw that broke the camel's back with this guy? He had one incident back in 2004. But are you going to dump Michael Phelps because of this picture? Smith: It could happen, and the reason why is because a lot of these companies that are sponsoring him really are focused on kids and how actions of their athletes affect children. So that can be a big problem. The other thing is, unlike an athlete that plays sports every year in the public spotlight, the Olympics for swimmers comes only every four years. So he doesn't have that chance to rehabilitate his image immediately like a lot of other athletes, a basketball player or a football player would. So companies might say, you know what, let's not work with Michael Phelps right now, because he doesn't really have a chance to redeem himself. A picture says a thousand words, and how can he fight that? Roberts: How could you turn this around? If you were his attorney, if you were advising him what would you do? Smith: The first thing I would suggest is a drug test. And I know that that's not required. And I also know that he's not really going to have a problem with swimming in 2012. But I would just show that hey, I'm clean, I'm doing great. The next thing I would do is go out there in the public and talk about the troubles with working with drugs and really show the public that you are not about drug use, you are not about doing bad things in public. You are only about supporting the rules of WADA, the World Anti-Doping Agency, and supporting their drug testing program. So you can show that, hey, this is a minor incident, not a big deal. And really what it's all about is remaining clean. Roberts: If you were to lay a bet, would you say anybody drops him? Smith: I would say he'll have some problems. I don't know if I would say that a big sponsor would drop him, but I would say that a more wholesome-oriented sponsor might.

# Phelps Faces Fallout After Bong Photo Surfaces

*CNN American Morning*

Olympic swimming icon Michael Phelps is facing scrutiny this week after a British tabloid published a photograph appearing to show the 14-time gold medalist smoking from a marijuana pipe at a party.

The image, first printed by *News of the World*, reportedly shows Phelps using a glass water pipe, commonly known as a bong, at a gathering held at the University of South Carolina in November.

Phelps, 23, issued a statement acknowledging the photo and apologizing for his behavior.

"I engaged in behavior which was regrettable and demonstrated bad judgment," Phelps said in the statement. "I'm 23 years old, and despite the successes I have had in the pool, I acted in a youthful and inappropriate way, not in a manner that people have come to expect from me. For this, I am sorry. I promise my fans and the public it will not happen again."

The swimmer, who won a record eight gold medals at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, has become one of the most marketable athletes in the world, with endorsement deals estimated to be worth millions.

To discuss the potential business impact, we spoke with sports attorney Ryan Smith.

## Interview Transcript

**AMERICAN MORNING:** Ryan, thanks for being with us. Let's get right to it. How much trouble is Michael Phelps in when it comes to his endorsement deals?

**RYAN SMITH:** Good morning. Well, the honest answer is it depends on the sponsors. Phelps has relationships with major brands—Speedo, Omega, Visa, Kellogg's, among others. Every one of those contracts almost certainly contains what we call a morality clause. That's a provision that allows a company to suspend or terminate a deal if the athlete engages in conduct that brings them into public disrepute.

**AMERICAN MORNING:** So these companies could walk away entirely?

**RYAN SMITH:** They could, legally speaking. But whether they will is a different question. Phelps is an enormously valuable asset. He's clean-cut, he's got that all-American image, and he's a proven winner. Companies invested in him because of that image. A photo like this damages the brand they bought into, but dropping him also means walking away from a huge marketing draw. Most sponsors are going to weigh public reaction very carefully before making any move.

**AMERICAN MORNING:** He apologized very quickly. Does that help him legally and in the court of public opinion?

**RYAN SMITH:** Absolutely, on both fronts. From a public relations standpoint, getting ahead of the story and taking responsibility is exactly the right play. He didn't deny it, he didn't make excuses, he called it bad judgment. That matters to sponsors who are deciding whether to stand by him. It signals that he understands the mistake and it's not part of a pattern. Contrast that with an athlete who denies, then gets caught in a lie—that's far more damaging.

**AMERICAN MORNING:** This isn't the first time Phelps has had a run-in. He had a DUI back in 2004. Does that history factor in?

**RYAN SMITH:** It does, and that's the real concern for his team. A single incident is a mistake. A second incident starts to look like a trend, and that's what sponsors fear most. If a company starts to believe this is who Phelps really is, rather than a one-time lapse, that changes the calculation. His camp is going to have to work hard to frame this as an isolated error in judgment, not evidence of a deeper problem.

**AMERICAN MORNING:** What about the legal side beyond endorsements? Could he face charges?

**RYAN SMITH:** That's a separate issue. Authorities in South Carolina could theoretically investigate, but proving a case based solely on a photograph is difficult. You'd need to establish where and when it happened, chain of custody of any evidence—it's not straightforward. I'd be surprised to see criminal charges stick from this alone. The bigger risk to Phelps is reputational and financial, not criminal.

**AMERICAN MORNING:** Bottom line—what's your prediction for his endorsement future?

**RYAN SMITH:** My guess is most of his major sponsors stay with him, at least for now. They'll issue statements expressing disappointment, they'll watch how the public responds, and they'll evaluate. Some may quietly not renew when contracts come up. Others may stand firmly behind him. But I don't expect a mass exodus. He's simply too valuable, and the apology bought him goodwill. That said, he's now on a very short leash. One more incident and this conversation gets a lot more serious.

**AMERICAN MORNING:** Sports attorney Ryan Smith, thank you.

**RYAN SMITH:** Thank you for having me.

---

*Phelps is scheduled to compete in upcoming events as he prepares for future international competition. CNN reached out to several of his sponsors for comment and will update this story as responses come in.*

# Mock News Transcript: Sports Law Analysis Segment

**[STUDIO - EVENING NEWS BROADCAST]**

---

**ANCHOR (Diana Reyes):** Good evening. Tonight we're examining a story that's dominated sports headlines this week. A prominent Olympic swimmer—whom we'll refer to generically as our subject, given ongoing developments—has been photographed in a situation involving recreational drug use. To help us understand the legal and commercial fallout, we're joined by sports law expert Professor Marcus Chen. Thank you for being here.

**PROF. CHEN:** Happy to be here, Diana.

**ANCHOR:** Let's start with the sponsorships. When an athlete is photographed like this, what actually happens contractually?

**PROF. CHEN:** Great question. Most major endorsement deals contain what we call "morality clauses" or "morals clauses." These give sponsors the right to suspend or terminate a contract if an athlete engages in conduct that brings them into public disrepute. So the first thing happening behind the scenes right now is that legal teams are reviewing the specific language of each contract.

**ANCHOR:** So it's not automatic that he loses everything?

**PROF. CHEN:** Correct. It depends heavily on the wording. Some clauses require a criminal conviction; others are triggered simply by negative publicity. A photograph alone, without charges, may not meet the threshold for termination in every contract—but sponsors often act preemptively to protect their brand.

**ANCHOR:** We've already seen two brands announce they're "pausing" their partnerships. Is that a legal move or a PR move?

**PROF. CHEN:** It's often both. "Pausing" is a strategic middle ground. It lets a company distance itself publicly while avoiding a costly termination that might later be challenged in arbitration if the facts turn out to be more complicated.

**ANCHOR:** What about his standing with the sport itself—could there be competitive consequences?

**PROF. CHEN:** That's a separate track. Recreational substances are handled differently from performance-enhancing drugs. Anti-doping agencies have specific rules about substances of abuse, and depending on the timing and whether it was in or out of competition, there could be a period of ineligibility—though these have been reduced in recent years if the athlete demonstrates it was unrelated to sport performance.

**ANCHOR:** And the public image dimension?

**PROF. CHEN:** This is where it gets interesting. Public perception often moves faster than any legal process. We've seen athletes rehabilitate their images successfully through accountability, treatment, and time. The ones who struggle are typically those who deny clear evidence. How he responds in the next 72 hours may matter more than any contract clause.

**ANCHOR:** Professor Chen, invaluable insight as always. Thank you.

**PROF. CHEN:** My pleasure.

**ANCHOR:** We'll continue following this story. After the break—

**[END SEGMENT]**

---

# Swimming Against the Current: Michael Phelps and the Photo That Sparked a National Conversation

*CNN Sports Special Report*

In February 2009, Olympic swimming legend Michael Phelps found himself at the center of controversy when a photograph published by a British tabloid showed him using a marijuana pipe at a University of South Carolina house party. The image, which surfaced just months after his historic eight-gold-medal performance at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, ignited debates about athlete conduct, sponsorship responsibilities, and America's drug policies.

CNN sat down with sports ethics experts, marketing analysts, and former athletes to unpack the fallout from one of the most talked-about celebrity controversies of the year.

---

## The Immediate Fallout

**CNN:** When the photo first surfaced, how significant was this story in the sports world?

**Sports Analyst:** It was massive. You have to remember the context. Phelps wasn't just any athlete—he had just become the most decorated Olympian in a single Games, capturing the imagination of the entire world. He was a genuine American hero. So when this image appeared, it was jarring precisely because it clashed so dramatically with the wholesome image he'd cultivated.

**CNN:** Did Phelps deny the allegations?

**Sports Analyst:** No, and I think that's important. He didn't try to dispute it or claim it was doctored. He issued a fairly swift apology, acknowledging that he had engaged in "regrettable behavior" and demonstrated "bad judgment." He described it as youthful indiscretion and promised it wouldn't happen again. That directness probably helped him in the long run.

---

## The Sponsorship Question

**CNN:** Phelps was one of the most marketable athletes in the world. How did his sponsors react?

**Marketing Analyst:** It was a mixed response, which is actually what made this case so interesting from a business perspective. Some sponsors stood firmly behind him. Speedo, for instance, publicly reaffirmed their support. Subway also maintained their relationship with him.

**CNN:** But not everyone stayed on board?

**Marketing Analyst:** Correct. Kellogg's made the decision not to renew their contract when it expired, stating that his behavior wasn't consistent with their image. That was probably the most significant commercial consequence he faced. It sent a message that even a superstar isn't immune to accountability.

**CNN:** Was Kellogg's decision seen as fair?

**Marketing Analyst:** It divided opinion. Some people felt it was appropriate corporate stewardship. Others thought it was excessive—even hypocritical—given that we're talking about a young man at a party, not a criminal enterprise. There was actually a notable public backlash against Kellogg's, with some consumer groups calling for boycotts.

---

## The Suspension

**CNN:** USA Swimming took action as well, correct?

**Sports Analyst:** Yes. USA Swimming suspended Phelps from competition for three months. They also withdrew their financial support during that period. In their statement, they emphasized that while it wasn't a violation that would typically warrant severe punishment under anti-doping rules—marijuana isn't a performance-enhancing drug—they felt they needed to send a message given his role model status.

**CNN:** Was that suspension controversial?

**Sports Analyst:** Some viewed it as largely symbolic, since there were no major competitions during that window anyway. Critics argued it was more about public relations than genuine discipline. Supporters said the governing body had a responsibility to uphold certain standards, especially for someone millions of young people looked up to.

---

## The Legal Dimension

**CNN:** Were there ever legal consequences for Phelps?

**Legal Correspondent:** This is where it gets interesting. The party took place in Richland County, South Carolina, and the local sheriff, Leon Lott, initially indicated he was considering pursuing charges. There was quite a bit of coverage about whether Phelps might actually be prosecuted.

**CNN:** What happened?

**Legal Correspondent:** Ultimately, no charges were filed against Phelps. Prosecutors determined they didn't have sufficient evidence—the photograph alone, without the actual substance being tested or seized, wasn't enough to bring a case. Several other people were arrested in connection with the investigation, but Phelps himself avoided prosecution. Many legal observers felt the sheriff's aggressive posture was more about making an example than pursuing genuine justice.

---

## The Broader Conversation

**CNN:** Beyond Phelps himself, did this incident spark larger discussions?

**Cultural Commentator:** Absolutely. This became a flashpoint for the ongoing debate about marijuana laws in America. Many people pointed out the disconnect between the severity of the public reaction and the reality that attitudes toward marijuana were rapidly evolving. This was 2009—we were still years away from widespread legalization, but the conversation was heating up.

**CNN:** Did Phelps become a symbol in that debate?

**Cultural Commentator:** Somewhat reluctantly, yes. Advocates for reform pointed to him as an example of how a single moment could disproportionately impact someone's life and reputation over something that a growing number of Americans didn't consider seriously harmful. Others used it as a teaching moment about responsibility and role models. He didn't ask to be a poster child for either side, but he became one anyway.

---

## The Redemption Narrative

**CNN:** How did Phelps ultimately recover from this?

**Sports Analyst:** Remarkably well, actually. His story became one of the great redemption arcs in sports. He returned to competition and continued to dominate. He competed in the 2012 London Olympics and again in the 2016 Rio Olympics, adding to his medal count and cementing his status as the greatest Olympian of all time.

**CNN:** What do you think allowed him to bounce back?

**Sports Analyst:** A few things. His genuine apology helped. His extraordinary talent meant that his athletic achievements eventually overshadowed the controversy. And frankly, the public tends to be forgiving of young people who make mistakes, especially when they own up to them. Over time, this incident became a footnote rather than a defining feature of his legacy.

---

## Lessons Learned

**CNN:** Looking back, what's the lasting takeaway from this episode?

# Morning News Segment: Sports Attorney Interview

**[STUDIO SETTING - "MORNING PULSE" NEWS PROGRAM]**

---

**HOST (Rachel Chen):** Welcome back to Morning Pulse. This morning we're discussing the developing story around the athlete's positive drug test and the fallout it's creating. Joining us is sports attorney Marcus Webb, who has represented professional athletes for over fifteen years. Marcus, thanks for being here.

**MARCUS WEBB:** Happy to be here, Rachel.

**HOST:** Let's start with the endorsement side of this. We're already hearing that two major sponsors are "reviewing their relationships." What does that actually mean legally?

**WEBB:** Great question. Nearly every modern endorsement contract contains what we call a "morals clause"—sometimes called a moral turpitude or conduct clause. These give the sponsor the right to suspend or terminate the deal if the athlete engages in conduct that brings them into "public disrepute" or damages the brand's reputation.

**HOST:** And a drug-related issue would trigger that?

**WEBB:** In most cases, yes. But it's not always automatic. The language matters enormously. Some clauses require a *criminal conviction*, while others are much broader and can be triggered by mere *allegations* or reputational harm. When I review these for a client, that specific wording determines whether the brand has an immediate exit or whether there's room to negotiate.

**HOST:** So a sponsor can't necessarily just walk away tomorrow?

**WEBB:** Not always cleanly. There may be notice requirements, cure periods, or arbitration provisions. Sophisticated athletes now negotiate *reciprocal* morals clauses too—protecting themselves if the sponsor's own conduct becomes problematic. It cuts both ways.

**HOST:** Let's talk about the human side. Beyond the legal contracts, this athlete's public image is taking a hit. What's your advice?

**WEBB:** The first 48 to 72 hours are critical, and honestly, the biggest mistake I see is athletes rushing to speak before they understand the facts. My advice is usually threefold.

**HOST:** Walk us through it.

**WEBB:** First—get the facts straight internally before saying anything publicly. If there's a legitimate explanation, a contaminated supplement, a prescribed medication, you want documentation before you make claims you can't support.

Second—take genuine accountability where it's warranted. The public is remarkably forgiving of people who own their mistakes and far less forgiving of those who deflect or blame others.

Third—demonstrate action, not just words. Entering a treatment program, working with anti-doping education, community involvement. Rehabilitation of an image has to be shown over time, not announced in a single press release.

**HOST:** Do these image-repair efforts actually help preserve the endorsement deals?

**WEBB:** They can, and this is something people underestimate. A sponsor's decision often comes down to a business calculation about future risk. If the athlete responds maturely and the public sentiment stabilizes, brands are frequently willing to stay in the relationship—maybe with a restructured deal, performance-based reinstatement, or a temporary suspension rather than full termination.

**HOST:** So the response to the crisis can influence the legal outcome?

**WEBB:** Absolutely. The contract sets the boundaries, but the athlete's behavior in the aftermath shapes how aggressively the other side enforces those boundaries. Good crisis management and good legal strategy aren't separate—they work together.

**HOST:** Final thought for athletes watching who want to protect themselves before something like this ever happens?

**WEBB:** Negotiate your contracts carefully, understand every clause before you sign, and build a team—legal, PR, and personal—*before* you're in a crisis, not during one. The athletes who weather these storms best are the ones who prepared for bad weather when the sun was shining.

**HOST:** Excellent advice. Marcus Webb, sports attorney—thank you for joining us this morning.

**WEBB:** My pleasure, Rachel.

**HOST:** We'll be right back after this break.

Sponsors have morality clauses in their contracts, and swimming's governing bodies have their own codes of conduct. ## Broader Implications

Phelps, who captured a record eight gold medals at the Beijing Olympics, has faced questions about his conduct before. The incident renewed discussion about the responsibilities carried by high-profile athletes who serve as role models to young fans.
